log: THE TIME AXIS IN CLOSED FORM -- and where it stops being valid
Overdamped is not a simplification here: a nucleosome in water sits at Reynolds ~1e-9, so
inertia is irrelevant and gamma u' = f - K u is the equation. In the eigenbasis every mode
relaxes independently, so any instant is one evaluation and the 10^9-timestep wall is gone.
THE TRICK: write the series around its ENDPOINT. u(t) = u_static - sum c_k exp(-t/tau_k).
The truncated part then multiplies a DECAYING exponential, so the high-frequency modes a
modal basis cannot represent are exactly the ones that have already finished relaxing --
and the endpoint comes from the two-level solver, which is accurate to 4e-6.
1KX5 no waters: 13625 atoms, 40875 DOF, 263765 springs
194 internal modes | relaxation times span 7.23 to 4.88e+04 (ratio 6.75e+03)
Units: spring constants are arbitrary and gamma = 1, so ABSOLUTE times are not physical.
The spectrum's SHAPE is, because it comes from connectivity. Times below are in units of
tau_slow, the slowest mode's relaxation time. No picosecond or microsecond claim is made.

THE ENDPOINT FIX WORKS. Writing the series around u_static removes the modal basis's
truncation error at long times entirely (0.0000 against 0.2025 for the
naive sum), which is what made a 200-mode basis unusable before.
AND THERE IS REAL DYNAMICS TO COMPUTE. Assuming the response is instantaneous is

information the static answer does not.
VALIDITY FLOOR, measured not assumed: the closed form misses at t/tau_slow = 0.003.
Below that the dropped high-frequency modes are still relaxing, so the truncation
is wrong there. Above it the method is exact for the price of one evaluation.
